"Learning Linux" distills down to two general areas -- familiarization with a distribution's user interface and getting your head around the underlying conceptual differences of the OS (how you do things but also why you do things a certain way).

The first part can be fairly easy. The user interface "look" isn't welded to the OS like it is with Windows. You can pick a "Windows-ish" look like the KDE desktop if you want. The "Kubuntu" distribution is a good start because a lot of things "just work right."

Getting your head around the under-the-hood bits can take a little more time. Check out TLDP.org for an old document called the "System Administrator's Guide". It's a bit dated but a good start in fundementals and historical rationale. A major "under-the-hood" difference between distros is the "package management system" that the distro uses. This is basically the preferred tool for installing and managing software. Debian-family distros (like Ubuntu/Kubuntu) and Red Hat-family distros (like Fedora and SuSE) tend to dominate the field but there are others. Picking a popular distro to start with makes it easier to find software you like and gets you going quickly. You can venture out once you get your bearings.

As for gaming, that's always been a rough spot with Linux but it's gotten a lot better. The most important thing for you as a Linux gamer is video card performance. nVidia has been the name of the game for years but has also caught a lot of hell for refusing to back off from their proprietary-only drivers. Other cards are supported with varying degrees of performance as well as non-proprietary drivers but I'm not up on the most current state there. The point in all of this is to say that, if you are going to require proprietary drivers, go with a distro that plays well with the notion and makes it easy to manage. Kubuntu does.

Lastly, DMCA and OpenSource purism feally cripple some distros (Red Hat, CentOS, Fedora) in getting things like DVD playback, video editing, etc..., working because they all are rely on rights-restricted codecs or such. Start with a non-US distro and save yourself some headache. Kubuntu and Linux Mint are great examples of distros that "just work" or require very little hassle.

Welcome to a brighter world. Once you get past a few bumps you won't look back.
